::: {#thm-monte-carlo-p-valid}
#### The Monte Carlo permutation p-value is valid

Let $Y$ be exchangeable under $H_0$ (@def-exchangeable),
and let $\hat p_{\text{perm}}$ be the [Monte Carlo permutation p-value](#def-monte-carlo-p-value) of $T(Y)$
from $B$ independent uniform permutations.
Then $\hat p_{\text{perm}}$ is a [valid p-value](multiple-testing.qmd#def-valid-p-value):

$$\Pr_{H_0}\paren{\hat p_{\text{perm}} \le u} \le u \quad \text{for every } u \in [0, 1].$$

:::

:::{#rem-source-monte-carlo-p-valid}
#### Source: The Monte Carlo permutation p-value is valid

Phipson and Smyth [-@phipson2010permutation] show that the Monte Carlo p-value with the added 1 is valid for random permutations.
The proof is omitted here.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#exm-monte-carlo-p-valid}
#### Validity in a small simulation

Simulate 2000 data sets of 20 independent standard Gaussian values, ten per group,
so that $H_0$ holds.
For each, compute $\hat p_{\text{perm}}$ of the absolute difference in means with $B = 99$:

```{r}
#| label: monte-carlo-p-valid
#| code-fold: false
set.seed(582)
in_group1 <- rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), each = 10)
abs_diff_means <- function(y, in1) abs(mean(y[in1]) - mean(y[!in1]))
p_hat <- replicate(2000, {
  y <- rnorm(20)
  t_obs <- abs_diff_means(y, in_group1)
  t_perm <- replicate(99, abs_diff_means(y, sample(in_group1)))
  (1 + sum(t_perm >= t_obs)) / 100
})
u <- c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1)
data.frame(
  u = u,
  fraction_p_at_most_u = sapply(u, function(x) mean(p_hat <= x))
)
```

With $B = 99$ the p-value takes the values $0.01, 0.02, \ldots, 1$,
and for a statistic with no ties each value has probability $0.01$ under $H_0$,
so $\Pr(\hat p_{\text{perm}} \le u) = u$ for $u$ in that grid.
The fractions are close to $u$, within simulation error.
Choosing $B + 1$ to be a round number such as 100 makes the grid easy to read.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#rem-plus-one}
#### Why add 1

Without the 1, a data set whose statistic exceeds all $B$ permuted statistics would get a p-value of 0,
which claims that the observed result is impossible under $H_0$.
Under $H_0$, with no ties, that happens with probability $1 / (B + 1)$,
because the observed statistic is equally likely to be any one of the $B + 1$ values it is compared with.
A p-value that equals 0 with positive probability is not valid.
With the 1, the smallest value of $\hat p_{\text{perm}}$ is $1 / (B + 1)$.
:::
